cards.text: That same day, King Xerxes gives Queen Esther the estate of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. SAME DAY, friend. Haman's house changed owners faster than I can pull a batch out of the oven.

cards.question: Mordecai the Jew now walks right into King Xerxes's presence, because Esther revealed his ___ to her.

cards.text: The king had taken something back from Haman. Now he hands it straight to Mordecai.

cards.question: What does King Xerxes hand Mordecai?
Then Esther makes a move of her own: she puts Mordecai in charge of Haman's estate.

cards.text: The ring, the estate, Mordecai's moving UP. But Haman's evil scheme against the Jews is still standing, and Esther goes to the king once again.

cards.question: Esther comes before King Xerxes again and falls at his feet ___.

cards.text: The king holds out the gold scepter toward Esther, and she gets up and stands before him. One little wave of that thing and you're off the floor, friend.
Then Esther opens with FOUR polite lines before she even gets to the ask. Friend, people ask the boss for a raise with less warm-up than that.

cards.question: After all that warm-up, what does Esther ask King Xerxes for?

answers.text: A royal guard for every Jew

cards.question: Esther tells King Xerxes why she's asking. What does she say?

answers.text: She can't bear to see her people destroyed
She's afraid of losing her place as queen
She wants Haman's name to be forgotten

cards.text: King Xerxes answers Esther and Mordecai. He points out he's already given Esther Haman's estate, and Haman was hanged on the gallows because he attacked the Jews.

cards.question: King Xerxes tells Esther and Mordecai they may write about the Jews in the king's ___ as they please, and seal it with the royal signet ___.
King Xerxes says a decree written in his name and sealed with his signet ring can be revoked later.

cards.text: No take-backs. Not even for the KING. It's like hitting send in the group chat and finding out there's no delete button.
At once, the royal scribes get summoned. It's the twenty-third day of the third month, the month of Sivan.

cards.question: The royal scribes sit down and record all of ___'s orders.

cards.text: Those orders go to the Jews and to the satraps, governors and princes of 127 provinces, from India to Cush. I've stamped some BIG batches in my day, friend, but 127 PROVINCES?

cards.question: Each province gets Mordecai's orders in its own script, and each people in its own language.

cards.text: Mordecai writes it all in King Xerxes's name and seals it with the royal signet ring. That ring is getting more work today than my oven timer.

cards.question: Now those letters have to reach every province. How does Mordecai send them out?
By Mordecai's letters, King Xerxes gives the Jews in every city a right. What is it?

answers.text: To leave the kingdom in peace
To hide inside the king's palace

cards.text: And the letters go further. The Jews may destroy any force of any people or province hostile to them, including women and children, and plunder their possessions.

cards.question: The edict sets one ___ day across all of King Xerxes's provinces: the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar.
A copy of the edict is published in every province for all the people. Why?

answers.text: So the Jews will be ready on that day
So the king can count all his people
So every governor will send tribute

cards.text: The couriers ride out in haste on their royal horses, pressed on by the king's command, and the edict goes out in the citadel of Susa too. Those horses took off like somebody yelled "THE COOKIES ARE BURNING!"

cards.question: Mordecai walks out from the king in royal garments of blue and white, with a large gold ___ and a purple ___ of fine linen.

cards.text: Blue, white, purple and a big gold crown. Friend, I wear the same apron every single day, and I suddenly feel VERY underdressed.

cards.question: When Mordecai walks out dressed like that, the city of Susa is thrown into confusion.

cards.text: For the Jews, it's a time of light and gladness, of joy and honor. Friend, I know a thing or two about light showing up after a long dark.
And it spreads. In every province and every city the king's edict reaches, the Jews have joy and gladness, with feasting and celebrating.

cards.question: Meanwhile, the fear of the Jews falls on many of the people of the land. What do they do?

answers.text: They rise up against the king

cards.text: And that's where we'll set it down for now. Keep that thirteenth day of Adar in mind, friend, because this story's not done.

findings.problem: The passage starts in the middle of the story, but the opening card gives no context. "That same day" points to nothing the baker has seen. The card never says that Haman's scheme to destroy the Jews was exposed or that Haman was just hanged. The second sentence goes to a joke instead of setting the scene.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on. If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "laughing" is silly. Esther is falling at the king's feet to beg for her people's lives, so no baker would seriously consider it. The card is left as a two-way choice.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: This story card only restates the answer to card 14, that the decree can't be revoked, and adds a joke. It tells no new part of the passage and doesn't move the baker forward.

rule.text: Every story card tells part of the passage. Jokes ride along on those cards.

findings.problem: The blank "single" adds no meaning, because the question already says "one ___ day." The card only tests BSB wording. It asks nothing the baker can reason about, such as the date or what the day is for.

rule.text: A blank is a word that matters to the meaning, never a word like "or," "and" or "he."

findings.problem: The card asks the baker to guess the exact items in Mordecai's outfit (crown or ring, robe or sash or belt). No earlier card lets the baker reason this out, so it is a guess at wording, not meaning.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "ring" for the first blank ("a large gold ___") is arguable. Mordecai was just given the king's signet ring in 8:2 and used it in 8:10, so a baker could argue he walks out with a gold ring.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: This story card only repeats the outfit from card 12 (blue, white, purple, gold crown) and adds a joke. It tells no new part of the passage. It's a recap card.

rule.text: Every story card tells part of the passage. Jokes ride along on those cards.
